items.passage: We are told that in old Beirut there was a language school whose classroom had once been a farmer's barn, and that the farmer, Rashid, still came each evening to sit at the back. One spring a surveyor from the city, Mehreen, arrived with chains and stakes and announced that the new road would pass straight through the classroom wall. The council had decided it in winter; no one had thought to ask the farmer or the students. Rashid said nothing that night. __The next evening he brought a lamp, a slate, and a sack of beans, and he asked Mehreen to teach him the word for 'line' in every language the school taught.__ She taught him seven. By the last lesson she had redrawn the road along the orchard's edge, and the students carved her seven words into the doorframe.

items.passage: 'Two bowls, extra scallions, like always,' Dariush called from the noodle stall, though Linh and I had not eaten there together in six years. She sat across from me at the folding table outside the strip mall in Ohio, holding the envelope I had found in our father's desk drawer: letters from her, one every birthday, none of which he had ever passed on to me. I had driven three hours rehearsing how angry I would be. Instead I noticed how carefully she kept her nails short, the way our mother used to, and how she slid me the larger bowl without being asked. When she apologized for him, not for herself, I almost corrected her. Then I watched Dariush wipe the counter in slow circles and decided the correction could wait.

Indifferent, since the narrator cares more about the noodles than the conversation.

items.passage: Reputations are stitched like coats, in rooms no customer sees. In the back room of the tailor's shop on Gold Avenue in Albuquerque, Elan found the ledger while hunting for a spool of gray thread. Every winter for eleven years, the landlord had been praised from the church steps for the warm coats he gave his poorest tenants. Every winter, in the tailor's cramped hand, the same coats were entered as unpaid. Takoda, the landlord's son, read the page over her shoulder and said nothing for a while. The town would go on admiring his father, no doubt, with the kind of sincerity that costs a town nothing. Elan returned the ledger to its shelf, and the two of them sat among the bolts of wool, listening to the old tailor's treadle beyond the curtain.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the landlord's reputation for generosity?
options: Admiring, since the narrator suggests the landlord truly earned the town's praise through charity.
Indifferent, since the narrator attends only to the ordinary work done in the tailor's back room.
Outraged, since the narrator openly demands that the town punish the landlord for his deceit.
Wryly skeptical, since the narrator hints that the praise rests on labor done by someone else.

items.passage:
Once, at the ferry steps where Kerala's waters turn,
I, Farhad, sat beside the boy I'd benched all spring,
Rohan, whose feet were quicker than my patience.
He watched the boats; I watched him and said nothing.
A schoolmaster, waiting with his bundled books,
had told me that same morning, half in passing,
'The swiftest colt is ruined by the whip.'
I turned the words like coins inside my pocket.
Now, when the horn called out across the backwater,
I found I wished to ask the boy his mind,
not tell him his mistakes, as I had always told him.
He rose and went aboard; I did not stop him,
but kept his seat beside me, warm and empty,
as herons settled low along the palms.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Rohan in the poem?
options: Remorseful and newly attentive, as the speaker comes to value hearing Rohan's view.
Coldly dismissive, as the speaker still believes Rohan deserves to stay on the bench.
Openly envious, as the speaker resents the speed Rohan shows on the playing field.
Fearful and anxious, as the speaker worries Rohan will complain to the schoolmaster.

items.passage: Camphor, iodine, and the warm dust of the ceiling fan: that was the smell of the night-shift pharmacy in Accra where my brother Obinna worked, and where, after our mother's burial, he and I, Bao, spread her letters across the counter between customers. We were searching for her groundnut soup. Surely, I said, a woman who wrote to us every week for nine years had set it down somewhere. She had not. She wrote instead of the price of tomatoes, the neighbor's quarrel, the color of the harmattan sky. 'Stir until it tells you,' one letter said, of something else entirely. I laughed at that, and then, to my surprise, I could not stop. Obinna counted out tablets for a night watchman while I read on, and I began to think she had left the recipe in us rather than on paper.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward her mother as revealed in the text?
options: Frustrated, because the mother's letters seem to have hidden the recipe from her children.
Fondly amused, because the narrator finds the mother's habits endearing rather than lacking.
Distant and formal, because the narrator treats the letters mainly as records of prices.
Guilty, because the narrator regrets never having asked the mother for the recipe directly.

items.passage: We stopped at the roadside diner outside Lagos because the lorry had a split tire and Aiko said no tire was worth arguing with on an empty stomach. I was eleven that year, and the cassava harvest had failed so thoroughly that my father had stopped speaking at supper. Aiko had been his friend since before I was born, and she had driven up from the coast to bring us seed for the next planting. While the mechanic worked, she ordered two plates of rice and ate hers slowly, asking me, Folasade, the names of every bird on the wires. I knew she was keeping me from crying. I also knew, even then, that she had sold her own sewing machine to pay for the seed, though she never said so. When the tire was fixed, she paid for both plates and let me carry the change.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Aiko in the text?
options: Puzzled, since the narrator cannot understand why Aiko chose to stop at the diner at all.
Resentful, since the narrator feels Aiko treated her like a small child during the delay.
Quietly grateful, since the narrator recognizes the care and sacrifice behind Aiko's actions.
Mildly bored, since the narrator mainly recalls the long wait for the mechanic to finish.

items.passage: Nguyen, my dear neighbor, I write this by the lamp while the last crates of grapes wait on your porch. You will tell me again that a man who sailed forty years can keep a little vineyard and a wine shop running on Chicago's South Side through one more winter. Perhaps he can. I watched you today on the ladder with your bad knee wrapped in sailcloth, singing the same three bars of a song you have never finished, and I had not the heart to call you down. Your sons write that the shop should close. I think they are sensible, and I think they have never seen you count the barrels as if they were stars to steer by. So I will carry the crates in tomorrow, and I will say nothing more of closing until the frost does. Your friend, Winifred
items.question: Which choice best describes the letter writer's attitude toward Nguyen's plan to keep the shop open?
options: Disapproving, as the writer urges Nguyen to follow his sons' advice and close the shop.
Envious, as the writer wishes she had a vineyard and a wine shop of her own to manage.
Detached, as the writer reports the harvest's progress without offering any opinion.
Affectionately torn, as the writer doubts the plan yet supports Nguyen's devotion to it.

items.passage: We have been three days on the barge down to Dhaka, and my grandson has taken to reading the cargo list aloud to the boatmen. This morning he found my old trunk among the jute bales and read the name painted on its lid: Clara. He asked who she was. I told him she was a girl who once learned English verbs at a mission school and believed she would never live anywhere but beside a cold sea. He said it was a pretty name and asked why no one says it. I could not answer him at once. Tonight I find I do not want the name back, exactly, yet I was glad, absurdly glad, to hear it spoken in his voice over the water. Chana I have been for fifty years, and Chana I shall stay; but I have asked him to leave the lid as it is.
items.question: Which choice best describes the diarist's attitude toward the name Clara?
options: Fondly nostalgic, cherishing the name's memory without wishing to take it back.
Bitterly regretful, wishing she had never given up the name of her girlhood.
Embarrassed, hoping her grandson will soon forget the name he read on the trunk.
Indifferent, treating the name as just one more entry on the barge's cargo list.

items.passage: Once, when I kept the hills above Lima and still believed every lost traveler was a fool, a hiker named Miriam came down out of the fog onto the village soccer field at dusk. She had wandered two days without a map. I meant to scold her, as I scolded all of them, and I had the speech ready. But she sat in the goalmouth and told the boys how she had followed the sound of their ball to find her way, and how she had shared her last bread with a stray dog that walked beside her. The boys listened as if to a saint. I listened too, and somewhere between the bread and the dog my speech went cold in my mouth. I lit the lantern, gave her my coat, and walked her down to the road myself, Dario the scold for once saying nothing.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Miriam over the course of the text?

Fearful, as the narrator suspects that Miriam is a spirit who has come out of the fog.
Envious, as the narrator wishes the village boys admired him as much as they admire her.

items.passage: Waiting rooms make liars of everyone. Marco had told Baoyu twice that he was fine, and she had told him twice that the surgery was routine. When his aunt's message arrived from Milan, offering a ticket and a room for as long as he wanted, he read it under the vending machine's glow and did not answer. Baoyu brought him tea he had not asked for and sat one chair away, as she always did. Near midnight a nurse called for family. Baoyu stood, then hesitated, as if unsure the word included her. Marco stood too, and walked beside her down the corridor. Outside the tall windows, the cranes along the river blinked red, one after another, patient as clocks.

items.passage: Years later I still remember the knife Budi gave me the spring after my grandfather died. I took it for an insult, a blade for a boy who could not yet hold one, and I left it rusting in a drawer. That summer I walked out alone to the abandoned orchard below Chiang Mai, where my grandfather's trees had gone wild with suckers and moss. Budi was there, pruning with an old knife exactly like mine. He showed me where to cut so a branch would fruit again, and he did not mention the drawer. By evening my hands were green with sap. A gecko clicked from the fence post, and somewhere down the hill a temple bell rang twice and stopped.

items.passage: Four guards, two gates, one rule: no one enters the cemetery after ten. Camila and I worked the north gate in Valparaiso that winter, and Anacleto worked the south. Our plan was simple. On the anniversary of his brother's death, I would log him as sick, and Camila would swear she had seen him go home. He would slip inside and sit at the grave until dawn. At midnight he came to our gate, looked at the logbook, and closed it. 'If I lie to get in,' he said, 'I'll be lying to him too.' He sat outside the bars instead, on the cold step, and we carried our thermos out to join him. Below us, the funicular cars hung motionless on their cables, and a ship's horn sounded once from the harbor.

items.passage: Tapping a cracked tuning fork against the piano lid, Father Kostas asked me, in the winter of 1912, to lead the boys' choir at the Easter vigil. I told him I had not set foot in his church for six years and did not mean to start for the sake of a hymn. He did not argue. He only asked whether I would play him the opening phrase anyway, and when I did, he hummed the second line under his breath, slightly flat, as he always had. I, Hasan, expected him to stop visiting the music room after that. Instead he arrived every Thursday through spring, bringing figs wrapped in newspaper, never once repeating his request, and we argued about Bach until the caretaker rattled his keys. Outside, the tram to Galata ground its wheels against the frozen rails.

When I asked what brought him, he said his wife had planted the tomatoes along the east wall, and that each year on the day she died he simply watered them and went home. I confess I thought it too small a gesture at first. Yet by the time the keeper arrived, I had folded our speech into my pocket, and I helped Stavros carry the can to the east wall before going to Father's bench. Your Radek. Odile, the elder, swore that a thief in a green cloak had taken their saffron at dusk. Zaynab, the younger, swore no one had entered at all, for she had watched the door the whole hour. Each went alone to the quiet library behind the mosque to ask the keeper of records who was right, and each was sent home with the same answer: come back together. When at last they did, Odile recalled the cloak brushing the back window, and Zaynab recalled the shutter she had never thought to check. Between them, the thief at last had a road. In the reading room, a cat slept on a ledger no one had opened in years.

Chinedu, who swept the hall each evening, had heard her mother coughing through their shared wall for three nights running. He remembered, too, that his own father had died in a village two days' ride away while Chinedu was here in the city, learning of it only by letter a month afterward.
